utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Please be seated. I can already see Madam Dahuron. But first of all, let's hear the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the third party, I can see the appearance of Madam Dahuron in Banja Luka. Good afternoon to Banja Luka once again. Let's have a sound check. Could you please speak.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Let's have the usual view around the room, and at the same time, please, escort the witness into your office. So proofing procedure or what's happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban, here from The Hague. Can you hear me in Banja Luka in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, please. And before starting with the examination, may I ask you, is it necessary to grant you any kind of protective measures, or are you prepared to testify in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against testifying in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You're called as a Defence witness, therefore, the floor is for the Defence. Mr. Ostojic will put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Mr. Branko Lukic, we represent Milomir Stakic. I'll be asking you a series of questions here today in connection with this case, and the information that you had provided to us previously. If at any time, sir, you do not understand my question, please state so, and I will attempt to clarify the question so that you may fully understand it and give us a truthful and complete answer. Is that a fair way to proceed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gruban, for the record, can you please state your full name, your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Dragoljub Gruban, son of, Krstan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were born, what municipality, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you were born and in which municipality does that town belong in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Maricka in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct to understand, sir, that throughout your entire life, you lived in the village or in the municipal -- municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: 1938, on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we, sir, have your father's name as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: My father's name is Krstan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just, if I can clarify, can you tell me who Stojan is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: My father's name is Krstan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, by way of background what profession were you engaged in at the time when you were gainfully employed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I was a worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us understand in what profession or area were you employed as a worker?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: While I was employed in Belgrade, I was a foreman at a forwarding agents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to speed things along a little bit, can you tell us in 1992, were you gainfully employed, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: In 1992, I wasn't gainfully employed. I stopped working in 1980, and I haven't worked since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly outline for us your educational background.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Just primary school. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you have children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many children you've had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Three sons and one daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all your children currently alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: No. One was killed on Gradacac in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for having to inquire a little further about your son who was killed in 1992. Was his name Marko Gruban?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, he was killed on the day -- on the anniversary of his birthday, correct? Essentially he was born on December 17th, 1971, and he died on December 17th, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My sincerest sympathies in connection with that, and I apologise for having to further inquire on this issue. But can you please tell us, how is it that your son ultimately --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- died?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I was at home. It was wartime. And in 1992, on the 17th of December, I experienced a shock when I saw the army -- the military bringing a coffin in front of my house. It was then that I realised it was my son when they showed him to me. Then I buried him, and to this day, I don't know how he was killed or what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was your son mobilised as a result of the war and the hostilities that were predominant in the region in 1991 and 1992, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: He didn't serve in the army because he had an eye defect. But in 1991, there was an amnesty, that's what it was called. And all those who were unfit to serve in the army were asked to come before a commission. The commission established that he was able to go to war, and the military police came and took him away. And they took him off to war in 1992. And after that, I never saw him again until they brought him home dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was there anything you, as a parent, that you were able to do in terms of exercising any influence to prevent your son from being mobilised and placed into battle in 1992, as you've so described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Well, I had two other sons. The eldest was Dragisa, he was on the Slavonian front. And I had another son Ljubisa, he was the middle one. He was in the Territorial Defence. The third son, because he was unfit, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. asked the military command that he be exempt. But as I have just told you, when he went for a checkup, they declared him fit and took him off. So that's how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that we can have a better appreciation, where was the military command, sir, that you went to to ask for your son to obtain an exemption because of his medical condition so that your youngest son, Marko, would not have to serve in the military? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: To Prijedor, to Kozara where the military was, to the military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you mean when you say "Kasarna"? Is that where it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the barracks. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your eldest son, Dragisa, as you've mentioned, was he, sir, also wounded in the war when he served in Slavonia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: He was wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your eldest son Dragisa serve in the military in any capacity any time after he was wounded in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your middle son Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he was a member of the Territorial Defence. Can you tell us to the extent that you recall for what period did he serve as a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: As he had had a kidney operation, they put him in the Territorial Defence. From 1992 until 1994, he remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the military that mobilised your son Ljubisa into the Territorial Defence, Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: It was done in the local commune that was in charge of the Territorial Defence in case a village had to be defended. And they were also in charge of collecting food and clothes for the soldiers on the front lines. And then they would take that to them and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, do you recall a period in May of 1992 when the Territorial Defence was abolished and that it was actually subsumed under and to be included as part of the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that now. I wasn't interested in things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, sir. Sir, I also note from my review that you are a member or president of an association of families of killed soldiers in the local commune in which you reside. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about this organisation, when it was formed, the purpose or mission of the organisation, and tell us a little bit about what you do within that organisation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: This organisation was established after the war in 1995. This organisation has a president in every local commune, and these make up the presidency. Our aim is to solve the problems of soldiers, of veterans, actually, to help them obtain housing, to help them construct homes. And to solve the problems of orphans, to assist them as far as we are able to. We dealt with a number of problems, problems that children or rather orphans and veterans had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to turn the topic slightly, if you don't mind, and I'm going to ask you whether or not you personally know Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when you first met his acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I knew him when he was a child. One of my sons was born in 1962, the same year he was born. They went to school together. And when I went to PTA meetings, I knew of him as a young boy. I knew him when he went to secondary school and when he was a student. And I know that when I was home for the holidays on weekends, we had voluntary road-building drives, and he was very active there. He would help us. We also worked on preparing sports fields, and he liked to play football, so he would come and help us in that. And that's how I knew him for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also, sir, have an opportunity to know Dr. Milomir Stakic's father, Milan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share with us your relationship with Milan Stakic, Dr. Stakic's father.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: He was very correct. We were of the same generation, and we were mobilised into the former army together. And as young men, we would look at the girls together. We respected each other. We never quarrelled. We never held any grudges against each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us to the extent that you're able, based upon the period of time that you knew Dr. Milomir Stakic, his character, reputation, and integrity, as you knew him and as it was perceived in the community.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Well, from my experience, I know that he was a decent young man. As I've just said, he went to school. He was a good boy. And when he was holding his office, I never heard people say anything but nice things about him. He was respectable. If people went to see him for some reason, he would receive them nicely. He was polite to them. I never heard anything bad about him. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, visiting Dr. Stakic after your son was brought from the military, after you learned of his death, after September [sic] 17th, 1992, to visit Dr. Stakic -- December 17th, 1992, to visit Dr. Stakic in connection with plans for the burial and funeral of your son?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you enlighten us and give us the circumstances of that visit, sir. Why did you go see Dr. Stakic? What was it you wanted to obtain, if anything, from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I went to ask for help with the funeral. But the military took charge of this. They donated a coffin and some food. Mr. Stakic also helped me, but I have already forgotten. There was some aid in food and in money. That was Yugoslav money, and it would be hard to calculate what the value was in German marks. But he did help me in my pain and suffering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, so that we can obtain a little better idea about Dr. Stakic's father, Milan, did he at any time that you knew him hold or have any nationalistic ideas or ideology?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if you're familiar with the iron ore mine in Omarska. Do you know that it's in existence, and specifically in 1992, do you know that it existed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course I know. It's a mine in Omarska which was opened for mining purposes and the facilities that they later called a camp was constructed for the repair and maintenance of the machinery used in the mine. That's what I knew. And I heard that it had been turned into a camp. But even when it was used for civilian purposes before the war, I was not able to enter it. But especially later when it became a camp, I was not able to enter it either, so I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say when the Rudnik iron ore mine facility was used for civilian purposes before the war, sir, are you telling us that prior to the war, the iron ore mine was used to manufacture and produce iron ore, correct, and that is what you mean when you say for civilian purposes? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the war started in the spring and summer of 1992, you mentioned that it was used as a camp. Do you know who used the facility as a camp? Who was using the facility as a camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I told you, I did not go near it, nor was I interested in it. It was wartime, and I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another couple questions on the background of Dr. Stakic and his father. Do you know if his grandfather, your friend Milan's father, whether he fought in World War II and in what capacity did he fight? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he participated in the war, when there was a war from 1941 to 1945. I had a brother, too, and that is Milan's father. And they were killed. My brother was killed in 1942. I wouldn't know when he was killed, but he did. It was the same army, everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which army was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: It was called the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So more specifically, sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Partizans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my question. Thank you for adding it. But just to the record is clear, was Milan Stakic's father a member of the Partizan group or the Chetnik group during World War II?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Partizans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1993, sir, did you have an opportunity to seek out Dr. Stakic again for any care and treatment to other members of your family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of that visit, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: I had my wife, Dusanka, and she fell and broke her hip, or leg, as we call it, at home. And she underwent the operation in Banja Luka. But when that was over, three months later after the treatment, she needed to go to a spa. So I asked Dr. Stakic to help me. Since it was wartime, I had no money. One couldn't get to a spa. And Mr. Stakic helped me as a doctor, as a physician, he wrote a recommendation so that my wife was granted 21 days of treatment in Miljecanici spa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was during the time that Dr. Stakic was employed and working at the health centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, on behalf of Dr. Stakic, we want to thank you for assisting us. And we have no further questions. But now, as is the procedure here, the Office of the Prosecution will put some questions to you, and the Court may as well. Once again, thank you, sir, for coming to help us in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I give now the floor to Ms. Sutherland, representative of the Prosecution in this case. Please, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban. I'm very sorry that you lost your son during 1992. And the Prosecution does not have any questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I've only one single question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been a neighbour of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Well, I've already said it. We are in a village which is called Gornja Maricka, and our house is about 3 kilometres apart, because houses in the village are quite scattered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's all. I thank you for this additional clarification. May I ask, Judge Vassylenko, do you have any further questions? No questions. Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban. Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you know about the creation or formation of a political group called the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB GRUBAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it remains for me to thank you, Mr. Gruban, for coming to the office and testifying in this case and assisting the Trial Chamber. Thank you, and you are excused for today. This concludes today's videoconference, and once again, thanks to all the persons who are assisting us in Banja Luka in establishing this videolink. Thank you, and until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can proceed now by hearing the next witness. As to the fact that we have to conclude at a quarter to 5.00, the next break will be an extraordinary short one. Therefore, the trial stays adjourned only until 3.20. And I would ask the usher, before the Bench comes back, already to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you. --- Break taken at 3.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Rosic, please be seated as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to thank you for coming another time. And let's just continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With Your Honour's leave, I will complete Mr. Koumjian's cross-examination due to his ill health.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, yesterday afternoon you gave evidence that approximately 20 or so buses arrived at the Omarska camp. Were those buses Autotransport Prijedor buses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked at the camp until August of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on other occasions when you saw detainees being brought to the camp, were they being brought to the camp also in Autotransport Prijedor buses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were more Autotransport Prijedor buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please understand that it is for us, the Judges, having never been in Prijedor, sometimes a little bit difficult to understand. And therefore some question may seem for you a very simple one. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But let's start with your testimony of yesterday. You told us about the arrival of buses, and then you shouldn't be confused, it's only for the purpose of our transcript, on page 50, LiveNote yesterday, line 15, you stated: "I only saw them when they arrived in buses. People were objecting, protesting. People didn't want them to be brought to the mine." Can you give us a more clear picture of what happened. Who were these people objecting? How did they object?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They protested saying that that would not be all right, that there would be more problems if people were brought there, as there were many people being brought there, and they were mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please tell me how did they know that these people brought in were mostly civilians, and why did they protest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They protested because they were being brought there. They were local people. They must have had certain suspicions that something was wrong with bringing all those people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many people were there protesting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know how many exactly, but that was the largest group of people, women and men in all these protests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it is still difficult for me to understand, how could they know in advance what was happening in there? The buses arriving, but the protesters already being there. How did they know beforehand what would happen, that the buses would arrive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the state of war had started. There was gunfire, and they realised that the situation wasn't quite as it should be. I'm really not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in a position to explain it properly. Well, it was practically the state of war, and people had certain doubts. They realised that something was wrong seeing that all those people were coming there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to, first of all, show me Exhibit S15-16 I think it was. Only that there is no misconception, we are referring now to S15-16 only, not -1. May the witness please be shown S15-16. May I ask you, Mr. Rosic, do you -- you can see what is depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows, I think, that they stopped at the very entrance, at the very front gate. That is where they stopped the buses. I think there are some buses, it seems to me, in front of this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in a little bit. Thank you. So if the witness --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a building. That's a building. Now I see it. That's a building where people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know the buildings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please be given a red marker. Could you please mark the place where the buses arrived. If I'm correct, and I apologise for the parties, to the best of my recollection, you yesterday said that when you arrived for the morning shift, the buses were already in front of the area and waiting for entrance. Would you show us where this was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the gate. There was a gate on this side, but you can't see it here. They were standing at the gate in a queue facing the building. But I just don't see that building. You can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be to the -- please indicate on the ELMO, if you could move to the other side, to your right-hand side, and with the marker show the direction from where the buses arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this direction, from -- I can see it better on the screen over there. But they came from this direction, the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the side of the administration building, there was the entrance, correct, and there the buses waiting when you arrived coming to work? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please -- I know that not the entire area is covered by this picture. But could you make -- mark the area from where the buses actually came with an E. Capital E, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you mean? Should I put it on the screen or...? Oh, here. Letter A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. For the transcript, it's marked with the letter A where, if I understand you, the buses waited in front of the entrance door when you arrived. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They were at the gate waiting, the front gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then you mentioned yesterday the place where your working place, in fact, was. Could you please mark this area or this house, if you can identify this, with a capital B.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building was above, at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In addition, yesterday you mentioned that you were warned to enter not a specific area because there would be mines, and it would be dangerous for you to enter this area. Could you please mark this area.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area was above the petrol pump, but I can't really see it well. Up next to the petrol pump, I can't get my bearings exactly where that is, where the petrol pump. There, they said it wasn't safe to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you indicate approximately the area where this was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know approximately because I can't really read this photograph well. I know the petrol pump, but I just can't say where it is. The petrol pump was somewhere up there, that direction, but I can't really -- I'm afraid to mark anything. If I had the whole view, then I'd be able to do that. But like this, on the screen...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be correct that on this picture, the area would be on the right-hand side, far more to the right of the place where you worked and that you marked with a B. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see armed police or military forces on the territory of this investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were military there. When the buses arrived, the troops arrived, too. And they were there looking after the civilians and those buses. When they got off, there were troops there. The troops brought them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know the question was already put to you yesterday. In the buses, there were only civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some soldiers, too, but there were also civilians. When they were getting off, I could see civilians and soldiers. But whether they were escorts or what, I don't know. But there were some soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that there were troops there. These troops, were they soldiers from the JNA, merely soldiers from the JNA, or also police forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know whether they were a part of the police forces or whether they were active-duty soldiers. But at any rate, they were military. I couldn't really say who's what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you remember the uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing uniforms, that is, olive-green-grey. That's the colour. I don't know whether you understand what it is. But it's olive-green-grey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please explain for us a little bit more what it means for you when they are wearing olive-green-grey uniforms? Because I asked were they part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were part of the units or not, but they wore the same uniforms because that is how they looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's continue a little bit. During the time these persons were detained in this centre, were there permanent posts stationed in or on the territory of this part of the Omarska previously ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When those buses came and when the troops got there, there were permanent guard posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And on the area, were there, for example, nests of soldiers armed with machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had guard posts around, around the compound, around that centre. They had their guard posts there. And what do I know? Of course they were armed. There were guard posts all around, naturally. All around the compound. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just coming back for a moment to the question of the areas you shouldn't enter, when working later in -- on the territory of Omarska ore mine, did you ever see that mines were dug out from this area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. Perhaps it wasn't done during my shift because there were other shifts. We changed. I did not see them taken out or put in. We were simply warned not to go there, not to take the road in that direction. We had the routes we covered, that is, going to our workplaces, and that was that. And that is where we moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you at any point in time later told, "It's no longer dangerous to enter this area because there are no longer such risks based on mines"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't told anything. For as long as the people were there, nobody ever said that we were free to move around there. I could move freely only to my workplace and the pumps that I've already described. They were about a thousand metres away, and sometimes I used a vehicle to get there. Sometimes I went on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, did you during the last days or weeks meet Mr. Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the witness be shown S15-16-1. And the other document with the marks, let's wait a minute whether we need it again. May I put to you, Mr. Rosic, that Mr. Vuleta when testifying here, he marked the areas where armed guards were located with a P, and areas where land mines, where there was a risk of land mines, with 3 lines you can see at the right-hand side of the picture. Showing you this picture is only for the purpose of a possible -- or for an attempt to refresh your recollection. So when you see these areas, especially where the police or military posts marked as P were located, do you recall that at these special points were armed forces in protection of especially the hangar but also the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At these concrete points where you can see four times the P. Correct? So it would be -- yes. Thank you, usher. If you could use this pointer, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please, then, because we want to have your own testimony, please may I ask the usher to put the other document we will mark as S15-16-2 once again on the ELMO. And could you please, with your red marker, mark these places where, to the best of your recollection - if you don't know, tell us - to the best of your recollection mark these places where you recall that armed forces were located, with a P, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a P?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. For the transcript, it's a Cyrillic P.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were around here. I didn't really pay much attention, but they were here and here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please, all the places you mentioned, mark with a P.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then a little further on. This whole compound here, there were military here. And that's the road. So on this side of the road, there were some here, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, with a P. You made only two -- yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I saw. They were around the compound, so I've marked the approximate locations. I can't be very precise, but there were trenches, and they were in a circle around the military -- around the building, around the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a special protection of the white house?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can see the white house here. There were police here. The military were around the compound, but there were more police inside where the detainees were. Mostly it was the police inside. And the military were around the compound. They had trenches there. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any, because I can understand your answer, therefore, in a more neutral way, any armed forces in the neighbourhood of the so-called hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the vicinity of the hangar, but around the hangar there were military. And inside, there were police securing the area around the hangar. And all around were the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And was there also such a special protection for the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know that it is - and you already mentioned due to the bad quality of this picture - that you can't exactly identify the area, but could you indicate approximately where the area was you were warned not to enter because of mines endangering your life and limb.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was somewhere up here, above the petrol pump. The petrol pump was on this side, somewhere up there. So it was above the petrol pump towards the area referred to as Gradina. They said we weren't allowed to move there. I didn't look at that place. I didn't go there. We weren't allowed to wander around and look around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please mark this with a C approximately where this area was, with a capital C.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, during your testimony, you mentioned several times areas where you wouldn't be allowed to go to. Where were these areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These areas were up above the petrol pump. We weren't allowed to move around there, either by day or by night. And that was in the direction of the place called Gradina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You also mentioned this when you were asked about women detained in Omarska. Where was this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness then be shown, please, Exhibit Number S15/18. This is the attempt for a reconstruction on the basis of a model in another courtroom. Can you identify the area, white house, administration building, hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Administration building. This was it. This is the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not a photo. It's a reproduction, an attempt of a reproduction. Maybe you can't identify the buildings there. Where would be the administrative building located vis-a-vis the hangar? I can understand that it's difficult for you to identify this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this very well. This is the little white house. I understand that. And this is the hangar. And this is the administration building, and the women were in the administration building upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's a little bit easier when you can have a look on the same model based on Exhibit Number S15-2. Can you identify the three buildings, hangar, white house --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the white house. This is the hangar. And this is the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the administrative building. I can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you know at which side of this -- to start another way around, were you allowed to enter the area between those two buildings? I think it was called the pista. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it was the pista. We weren't allowed to walk around there. We weren't. We had our workplace where we were allowed to move, but we were not allowed to walk around here. Only around the edges if we had to pass through in order to fix something. But we weren't allowed to walk around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you allowed to walk around the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you allowed to walk around the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only if it was really necessary. Sometimes it was really necessary because something had broken down and we had to repair it. In that case, we had to go there to fix something, something to do with water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see children in one of these buildings detained?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that you were aware that women were detained, and they were detained separately in the administrative building. Could you please with the pointer --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please with the pointer show us where in the administrative building this was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was upstairs in the administrative building. I don't know how I can mark that. They were upstairs, and they had separate quarters, the women did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And where was it, where was the place where you took, say, breakfast, lunch, and dinner?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had lunch in our canteen in the administrative building. That's where the detainees went. They always went in a line. They had two meals a day. And that's how they went. I know that's how it was. They went in a column to the administrative building where we had a canteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you also see women going to this canteen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see women going there. The women were held separately, and I think that food was brought up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where did you, yourself, take breakfast, lunch, and dinner?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we had that, and sometimes we went up there where the kitchen was in the little TAM truck. Sometimes they would bring it to us, and sometimes we would go there for lunch. It was about 2 kilometres away in Omarska, the pit where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see -- you mentioned just a moment ago the little TAM truck. Apparently it was called Tamici, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tamic, yes, we had a Tamic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see people bringing meal to the canteen with this Tamici?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes they brought it in the Tamic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that you saw several times corpses on the territory of the Omarska ore mine. How were they brought --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion only, a few corpses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse you, but wasn't it yesterday that you mentioned it once in connection with the events connected to Mr. Kvocka, and then later - I just try to find the exact page number and I come back to this. But how was it that the corpses, be it now one or more or several times, were transported away? Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a long time ago, but sometimes we recall incidents because of their special importance. Did you ever see delegations arriving in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us which kind of delegations this was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of delegations they were, but I know they came. They had a small bus of their own, and they came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was, in summer in 1992, in autumn, or in spring -- not in spring, of course. In summer 1992, immediately after the first buses arrived, or more close to that period when this area was no longer used as a Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the area was used as a Detention Centre, that's when they came. Later on, I didn't see any delegations arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there one delegation or were there several delegations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were some, but I don't know how many. I know that they used to come, but I don't know who came or why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You didn't know any of these persons arriving with the bus, correct, or...?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see high-ranking persons, be it military personnel or civilian persons of political importance, arriving in or being on this territory of the Omarska ore mine in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. Those very important persons, whoever came, I did not see them. Because I couldn't really keep up with it. I had accommodation of my own, and I had my job to do. So I wasn't there on those days because the pumps I maintained are far away. And I had to go there. I had no time to watch who's coming, who's going, and things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Final question: Did your son socialise with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, they were practically school fellows, peers. So yes, they socialised. They were good colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not your son had contact with Dr. Stakic in this period of time, say, from May 1992 to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not much, because he was absent. He was also on the front. He was with the police in Banja Luka, so he was absent. He was away. And he also went to the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I personally have no further questions. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, can you tell us how many buildings belonging to Omarska mine served as camp facilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As camp facilities, well, they were almost all full, and there were also some on the pista. It was summer. It was hot. And so they were also between the buildings on the pista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What were these buildings used for before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those -- before the conflict, those buildings housed workshops, depots for dump trucks, for caterpillars. We had some American machinery, and they were kept inside. And then, when it was necessary to put people in there, those machines were taken out of the hangar. So it was for machines there. And so there were people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How many buses arrived at the Omarska mine, and how many detainees were brought in in the first day when you saw this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the number. There were a number of buses, over 20. On the average, on the average, must have been a thousand -- over a thousand people. Must have been something like that. I've got a sore throat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you think, was it possible to detain so many people in these buildings without preparing them to serve as detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used them. They had to be used. They were not envisaged. But since they had to be used, they were used for it. The conditions were not good, but whatever you had, you had to put somewhere those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. You told us yesterday that you were made to use an armband, a white armband, to distinguish the workers at the Omarska mine and the detainees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Who told you to put on that armband?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our superiors said that we had to have some markings because we were moving about there, so that the military could know who we were, because there were civilians there, too, so that they wouldn't confuse us with others. Because we moved about, we came and went, and we had to have something. So we were ordered to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Was one of your superiors Mr. Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Was he who told you to use the armband?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: He was the one who was in charge in Omarska mine ore buildings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you know how the military told them they were going to use the facilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But he told you about the armband the first day the detainees were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Then yesterday, you told us, and for the parties and ourselves, it was page 54, line 10 more or less. My LiveNotes were down, so I'm not very sure. But you told us that you had the same food as the detainees. Can you just tell us what kind of food you got.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't say it was really good. It wasn't that good. But we who worked there, we also bought something extra or brought from home so that it was enough. But it wasn't really anything to write home about. There was a general crisis with food and all that, there was general crisis. The food wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the goodness or not. Can you tell me, for instance, what you get any day for lunch?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that is how it was. I can't really know it, whether people had the same food for dinner as they had for lunch. Is that what you're asking me? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No. I want to know if you were given soup or a stew or any other thing, fruit, vegetables. I don't know. Just tell me what you were given one day or the others.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. There would be soup at times, and then it would be beans. Do you know what that is? Well, at times, there would be beans. And it wasn't much of a food, but one had to eat. It wasn't really of a particular -- particularly good. The food was rather bad, not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just as a follow up, in fact, on yesterday's LiveNote, page 54, line 10, you stated: "Yes, yes, we had the same food." May I ask you following the other questions of today, where you yourself took the meal and where the detainees got the meal, how can you know you got the same food as the detainees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were getting the same food because there was only one kitchen. There was only one kitchen preparing food for everybody except that we had more. Sometimes from the same kitchen, sometimes the Tamic would bring food for us, or the same delivery van would take it to Omarska. It was some kilometres away where the kitchen was. So we ate the same food. It was the same kitchen for everybody. They prepared 5, 6, a thousand meals for everybody. And that is what we used. We were few, we were only 5 or 6; 2, 3 per shift. That's how many we were. So how could anyone prepare food for us separately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this, your conclusion. And I have to apologise that I didn't find immediately beforehand when asking you the question on corpses in the Detention Centre. On page 54 of today's transcript, you were asked about the events involving Mr. Kvocka. And then on page 55, related to this, line 1, you answered: "There were dead and wounded. I could see that. They took the wounded for treatment. Kvocka called in an ambulance. So he sent the wounded people off to hospital. That's what I know about it." Question by Mr. Koumjian: "At other occasions, did you have the unfortunate opportunity to view dead corpses or bodies in or around the iron ore mine in the spring and summer 1992?" And your answer was: "Yes, yes, I did see a few corpses." Could you please try to be a little bit more concrete on this question. How many corpses or dead bodies did you see and where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them over there, somewhere above the white house where people were lying down. Not many, two, three, men. And I was passing by going towards the pump, and that is how I saw them. And I got to the pump. That is how I saw those couple of people. And I did not see any more people there, and somebody must have picked them up because I did not see them again. That is what I saw. After that, I did not see it except during that incident with Kvocka, when there were a couple of people dead and some wounded. And Kvocka called the ambulance and took people immediately for treatment. And that was that. And there were a couple of dead. Had Kvocka not stopped it, there would have been more. And that is how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to these dead bodies you saw in the neighbourhood of the white house, did you discuss with some of your colleagues the reasons why there were these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really aware of that, why that was. But some people said they had tried to escape, and so fire was opened on them. That's something that I heard. But I didn't really know it for a fact. Those people who indeed tried to escape, and that was why fire was opened on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have no further questions. It is now the time for the Defence, re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. I have several questions I'd like to clarify if I may. First of all, the Honourable Judge Argibay asked you on page 30, lines 21 through 22 today with respect to a gentleman by the name of Mirko Babic. Can you just tell us, when the Court asked you whether Mirko Babic was in charge of the iron ore mine at Omarska, is it true, sir, that Mirko Babic was your superior and only the superior of those people who had previously worked at iron ore mine at Rudnik or Omarska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mirko Babic was not at any time and specifically was not during the spring and summer of 1992 in charge of either the police or the military at the iron ore mine at Rudnik or Omarska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. He wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify it. Sir, you had a picture that was shared or shown to you on the ELMO by the Honourable President Judge Schomburg earlier this afternoon. Just so that I can understand, I'm not going to ask you to compare the testimony, but was the initial -- when you examined the picture, the initial inside perimeter of the iron ore mine, was that in essence secured by the police and the outer perimeter secured by the military?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I have a clear record, you marked for military on that chart that you have with the Cyrillic letter P. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps with the Court's permission, we can just have that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be S15-16-2. And to the best of my recollection, the witness was asked to mark those places where armed forces, without any distinction between police and military was made. But please, for a better definition, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, I just would like to reserve my right to discuss that with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So as not to confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this exhibit that you have in front of you, you marked the areas with the -- and you've marked several places on this exhibit as I note. But with the Cyrillic P, you've marked areas on this exhibit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correctly marked around it. It was the military, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Where was the police, sir, in that diagram during the spring and summer of 1992 when the detainees were in the iron ore mine at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the hangar, around the mine. Around the prisoners. That's where they were. The police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they on the inside of where the military was, or on the outside of the military? How about I do it this way: Let me try it this way, and I might expedite it. With the Court's permission, can you mark, if I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, admittedly I myself didn't understand your question. So it would be helpful if we could mark the police, if you agree, with an S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As long as the record so reflects, Your Honour. That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please continue. And maybe it's of assistance if the witness immediately would be so kind and mark those places where the police was located with an S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, yes, the usher will hand you a pen, and if you would be kind enough to mark with a letter S -- the pen to your right which is red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, if you could indicate the areas where to the best of your recollection police was stationed, with an S always.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the hangar building, where the prisoners were. That's where the police was. Right next to the hangar building, around it. And then around them were the army troops. I've already said it. I can explain it like that, but I can also mark it. They were around the building. The police were around the building. And they were where I've already marked, the military were around them. That is where they had trenches, and they were in the trenches practically. That's how I saw them. And the police was inside -- I mean, within the camp around the detainees. They escorted them to lunch and back because they always walked a line to lunch and back. Of course, in rounds because there were too many of them. So one group goes and comes back, and then another group goes and comes back. And it was by and large the police who looked after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rosic. Just if you can quickly write with the letter S the approximate areas where you recall the police were during the spring and summer at the iron ore mine, spring and summer of 1992 obviously.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript once again, it's marked with a Cyrillic S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] S Cyrillic, that's where the police was. And here was the army. That was quite clear. No problem whatsoever. I saw them. I saw this area. I know it by heart. And what I saw I'm saying. But I can't really say exactly because I'm not a designer. I couldn't design this building. I'm not qualified for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's already an excellent painting. Only that the transcript is clear, you, in addition, marked with a Cyrillic C, which on my screen could read as an O, police in front of the administrative building. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, if you may, just follow the picture with me. You see the large building to the centre of the picture in front of you. That's the hangar. To the left is the administrative building, correct? And is it fair to say to the left of the administrative building is where the gate and entrance is to the iron ore mine as it existed in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just several questions if I may: Do you recall, sir, on the first day that the detainees were brought to the iron ore mine whether or not the military had a confrontation and a discussion with personnel from the iron ore mine as to whether or not they can gain access to the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, nor did I ask anyone. I didn't ask anyone. The military, they just got there without anyone ordering them to that. They never asked us. They were not under us anyway. They did what had to do. The army came, put people there and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir prior to the conflict in the area in the spring and summer of 1992, is it true that the iron ore mine had its own security guards and personnel to protect it from outsiders coming into the iron ore mine who were stationed at the gate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly how it was. We called them doormen. We called them janitors or doormen. They were -- they had their workplaces in different areas. Yes, but they were guarding, but they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those doormen or these janitors who were at the gate, the entrance, did you hear from anyone, sir, at any time that these doormen resisted the military when they first came and attempted to gain access in the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992 when they brought the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's true. It's already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to debate it right now, Judge, but I think we've just had a little bit of a communication problem with the witness in this regard. But in terms of exactly identifying them as either doormen or guards, and the witness clearly stating it wasn't people within. But certainly they were the doormen and the janitors who were at the gate. But to the extent that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have all understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir - thank you, Mr. Rosic - with respect to the detainees that were brought to the iron ore mine, you mentioned that some were in military clothes and some were in civilian clothes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The detainees that were brought in the iron ore mine, did they have the military uniform of the Territorial Defence to the extent that you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. I think they were the olive-green-grey, the SMB uniforms, but I didn't really see if it was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You used an abbreviation, SMB. Only that the transcript is clear, could you please tell us what it stands for, SMB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, for the witness. Because the witness used an abbreviation, and therefore we need the exact word. Could you please be so kind, Mr. Rosic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do I know? I wrote it just formally, just a dash, so that one can follow more or less. But I didn't really follow it very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood me. You used yourself the abbreviation SMB. And I wanted to ask you, what is the meaning of SMB, this abbreviation? What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SMB is the acronym. It stands for a colour which is dark green or how shall I call it, it is short for it. The so-called SMB uniform. I don't really know how to put it. I don't quite understand it. But it was dark green. A bit dark. But that is what we called it, SMB. I see you don't understand, but as a matter of fact, I don't understand it either. But I just thought I'd say it to help. But it's very difficult to really make up one's mind how it all was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we are in full agreement, but please, let us know who normally wore these SMB uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a military uniform. It was the military who wore that uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two more questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that the time is running late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that the Territorial Defence also wore those uniforms? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you allowed -- were you allowed or permitted to go into the actual offices in the buildings where the detainees were being held?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't allowed to go in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions, and I appreciate your patience. Can you just describe for us looking at the exhibit that's on the ELMO, how far away is the gate and the entrance to the administrative building that's depicted on this picture? How far away is it on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's maybe some 30 metres away. I don't know that it's more. About 30 metres. I didn't measure it, but I think that's the distance to the main gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were these janitors or men who were at the gate, the men who were allowing people to come into the gate prior to the conflict in 1992? How far away were they from the actual administrative building and the hangar as depicted in the picture?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends. They weren't all at a certain distance. They were at the gate. There were several of these men around the compound. Some were closer, and some were further away. They weren't all the same distance from the administration building. Wherever there was a need for a doorman, that's where he was. There were several places for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're just having trouble understanding this, and I know it's late and it's my fault because I've rushed the questions. Where, sir, is the separation between the actual premises of the iron ore mine or as you call it separacija from the iron ore mine and to where the outside roads would lead, how far away is that, the outside perimeter, if you will?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The separacija was about 2 kilometres away, 2.000 metres. I knew that was the distance because there was water there to wash the iron ore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that separacija that you have just mentioned 2 kilometres away, is that the area where these protests as you've described them occurred from the civilians who wanted to complain about the military utilising the iron ore mine as a detention facility in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People did protest up there at the gate. There was a gate at the separacija. And people protested there objecting to these people being brought to Omarska because we didn't find this acceptable. And people saw that this would not be a good thing bringing people in. But the military wouldn't listen. They forced their way in. They did what they wanted to do. They set up their military command there, and civilians were not asked anything. They didn't ask the doormen anything. They came in, and then there was nothing to be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rosic. Thank you for the extra time. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. And I have a request at the end, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At this point, it would for the Prosecution if there are any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are a number. I don't know whether I will finish before 5.00, I can certainly try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to exert any pressure, and if we can't to conclude the witness' testimony today, I would to give the Defence the chance. They were in a hurry apparently to proceed with their line of questions, if necessary. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When I say a number, I mean five. But it depends if I get quick answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try. Let's try, please. Further cross-examination by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, these people you mentioned earlier at the beginning of your testimony today that they were local people who were objecting to these 20 buses coming to the camp, were you talking about local residents from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the local residents. The residents of Omarska. It was them, no one else, because it was their area, and they found this objectionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also drew on a diagram, Exhibit 15-16-2, and you marked with a letter B the place where you said that you worked. Is it correct that you worked in the electrical workshop?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We were there. That's where our designated place was. And we had the best access there, and nobody hindered us in any way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Isn't the electrical workshop on the ground floor of the hangar building? As you enter the hangar building, you turn right, and it's in the corner of the ground floor of the hangar building.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the diagram this afternoon, the B you drew was outside towards the back right-hand corner of the hangar building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't exactly in the corner, but it was close to the corner, quite close to the corner. But I couldn't mark it any more clearly. It was towards the end of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you're standing at the white house looking towards the hangar building, the electrical workshop is on your right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but quite far away, quite far away. Far away from the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but on the ground floor inside the hangar building.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago on page 27 that you used to visit the pumps and that they were a certain distance away from the camp. Who were you visiting the pumps with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the pumps, and there was always someone going with me. And sometimes they would drive me there in the Tamic, in the little truck. And when they could, they would drive me there in the Tamic truck or I would --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there. Who were the names of the people that you went to the water pumps with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their names were -- there was a Stakic driving the truck. We called him Mico, Milorad or whatever. We called him Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the names of anyone else that you went with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC [Resumed]
